proposals.relationship: Wood questions Morgan’s emphasis on assigning responsibility and recovering the revolutionaries’ declared constitutional motives.
proposals.evidence_note: Own1966 essay treats Morgan and Jack P. Greene as named examples of neo-Whig limits while calling restoration of the importance of ideas necessary and refreshing. It argues that judging motives and responsibility misses unintended processes and some emotional beliefs. This is qualified methodological criticism, not dismissal of Morgan’s scholarship. Original journal scan checked; no attribution of later reprint annotations to1966.
primary_locators: Original1966 printed18–20, paragraph In attempting to rebut through the discussion before In his recent analysis; notes36–38 identify Morgan1957 and Birth of the Republic1956.

proposals.relationship: Morgan accepts Wood’s social-revolution thesis while questioning his magnification of changes in labor, royal patronage and loyalist departures.
proposals.evidence_note: Signed1992 review distinguishes persuasive central interpretation from overstated detail. Morgan invokes earlier Protestant valuation of work and the limited extent of royal patronage, and ends by endorsing the egalitarian transformation. Wood’s entire Radicalism was not read; no claim of blanket rejection.
primary_locators: HTML paragraphs beginning It is possible to fault through When every exception has been taken, followed by final three paragraphs.

proposals.relationship: Wood questions Greene’s concentration on conscious constitutional motives and later psychological explanations of the American Revolution.
proposals.evidence_note: Own1966 critique of neo-Whig historical explanation names Greene alongside Morgan, with necessary corrective credit retained. Own1982 opening identifies Greene’s Search for Identity1970 and Uneasy Connection1973 as examples of psychological readings that Wood seeks to replace with a wider account of eighteenth-century causal beliefs. Neither claim means every Greene interpretation was rejected.
primary_locators: Original1966 printed18–20, notes36,38; original1982 printed401–402, notes1,5–6 and406–409 wider-culture alternative.

proposals.relationship: Wood uses Greene’s account of colonial legislative independence when reconstructing Americans’ experience of divided authority.
proposals.evidence_note: Own2011 review credits Greene’s prominence and uses his account of colonial and Irish legislatures. Wood simultaneously argues that earlier local arrangements require more attention. The p707 description partly quotes LaCroix’s presentation of Greene; independent use at710/n13 makes the resource specific. Greene’s books and LaCroix’s full monograph unread; no formative influence claim.
primary_locators: Printed707 paragraph Most prominent, withn4; printed710 paragraph Parliament, according to Jack P. Greene and other scholars, withn13 citing Peripheries and Center1986p63.

proposals.relationship: Wood borrows Pocock’s formulation of a Namierian history of ideas to characterize Bailyn’s analysis of revolutionary thought.
proposals.evidence_note: Own1966 applies a specifically credited analytical formulation across the21–22 page break, n41 citing Pocock’s1965 articlep550. This is a small conceptual resource, not evidence that Wood adopted the whole later republican synthesis or a claim that Pocock coined every underlying idea. Pocock’s original article unread.

proposals.relationship: Wood questions the explanatory limits and fixed republican categories of Pocock’s synthesis.
proposals.evidence_note: Own1985 review of Diggins distinguishes Pocock’s synthesis from Diggins’s polemic. Wood questions its account of liberal America and objects to rigid categories, while recognizing its impact. He also reports Pocock’s self-qualification. Full Pocock and Diggins books unread.

proposals.relationship: Wood uses Hofstadter’s description of conspiratorial explanation as personal causation to develop his own historical account.
proposals.evidence_note: Own1982 essay explicitly takes up Hofstadter’s account of deliberate individual will when analyzing eighteenth-century causal assumptions. This conceptual use coexists with a challenge to its application across periods. Wood preserves possible modern applicability at his conclusion; full Hofstadter book unread.
primary_locators: Printed408–409, paragraph To understand how reasonable people through suspend our modern understanding, withn22 citing Hofstadter1965pp36,32,27; final441.

proposals.relationship: Wood challenges extending Hofstadter’s pathological and marginal model to widespread eighteenth-century beliefs.
proposals.evidence_note: Own1982 distinguishes Hofstadter’s expressly metaphorical usage from clinical diagnosis and acknowledges that Hofstadter omitted the Revolution. Wood argues that contemporary rational causality made conspiratorial beliefs broadly intelligible, while allowing a different modern assessment at441. This is a contextual limit, not rejection of all Hofstadter’s analysis.
primary_locators: Printed403–405, especially404metaphor/pathology distinction;407–409 cultural ubiquity and causal reasoning;441final two paragraphs.

proposals.relationship: Wood questions Davis’s linkage of revolutionary experience to a recurring American pattern of conspiratorial fear.
proposals.evidence_note: Own1982p405 identifies Davis’s question about revolutionary national identity; Wood’s following alternative relocates such thinking in wider eighteenth-century causal assumptions. He calls Davis meticulous and retains Davis’s warning against reducing every fear to internal psychology at404. This qualifies the explanatory framing; it does not accuse Davis of clinical diagnosis or reject his whole slavery history.

proposals.relationship: Wood questions Taylor’s treatment of captive violence and the narrative scale of The Divided Ground while praising its research and cultural analysis.

proposals.relationship: Wood objects that Turner’s1895 account of American origins leaves Indigenous people outside its historical explanation.
proposals.evidence_note: Own2006 review singles out Turner’s first-issue AHR essay and contrasts it with later histories treating Indigenous people as participants. This is Wood’s criticism of a specified older text, not direct re-reading of Turner’s essay or a claim about every work Turner wrote.
